title: Governança Corporativa: como o controle de cartões individuais prepara sua empresa para auditorias e garante compliance financeiro
summary: Entenda como otimizar a governança corporativa de custos. Controle despesas por API e prepare sua empresa para auditorias rigorosas com o Stark Bank
body_text: Entenda como otimizar a governança corporativa de custos. Controle despesas por API e prepare sua empresa para auditorias rigorosas com o Stark Bank Toda empresa em crescimento enfrenta o mesmo desafio: quanto mais transações, mais difícil controlar. Gastos de viagem aprovados informalmente, compras feitas com cartões pessoais e notas fiscais acumuladas em gavetas comprometem a conformidade da empresa e têm impacto direto no processo de auditoria. Por isso, neste artigo, mostramos o que é a governança corporativa aplicada à tesouraria e como seus cinco pilares fundamentais se traduzem em processos concretos de gestão de despesas. Também exploramos por que o modelo tradicional de reembolso falha em auditorias e como cartões corporativos individuais geridos por API atuam como ferramentas ativas de compliance. Confira! O que é governança corporativa no cenário financeiro de scaleups e enterprise? No contexto da tesouraria, governança corporativa é o conjunto de políticas, processos e ferramentas que define quem pode gastar, quanto, em quê e com quais evidências. Trata-se de controle financeiro a fim de garantir que cada real movimentado seja rastreável, autorizado e conciliável. Para empresas em crescimento acelerado, muitas vezes essa estrutura acaba sendo negligenciada: o foco vai para a velocidade de expansão, e os controles internos ficam para depois. O problema é que o “depois” muitas vezes coincide com a chegada de um investidor exigente ou uma auditoria, momento em que a falta de rastreabilidade se transforma em passivo contábil. Por isso, crescer sem governança não é uma opção sustentável. Os 5 princípios da governança corporativa aplicados à gestão de despesas O Instituto Brasileiro de Governança Corporativa (IBGC) define cinco pilares fundamentais para a governança corporativa: Transparência, Equidade, Responsabilização (Accountability), Sustentabilidade e Integridade. Na prática da tesouraria, cada um deles tem impacto direto no dia a dia de quem gerencia gastos corporativos. Transparência: o time financeiro tem visibilidade em tempo real de onde o dinheiro está sendo gasto? Equidade: todos os colaboradores têm acesso a ferramentas adequadas para realizar compras corporativas sem precisar usar recursos próprios? Responsabilização (Accountability): é possível rastrear cada transação com documentação confiável e auditável, e prestar contas dela de forma clara e tempestiva? Sustentabilidade: a empresa tem visibilidade de como os gastos corporativos impactam sua viabilidade econômico-financeira no curto, médio e longo prazo? Integridade: a empresa tem políticas claras que evitam decisões de compra sob conflito de interesses, associando gastos a centros de custo e responsáveis? A maioria das empresas consegue responder “sim” para algum desses pilares. Poucas conseguem para todos, e é exatamente essa lacuna que compromete o compliance financeiro. Transparência e Equidade no controle de tesouraria de alta performance A falta de transparência no controle de despesas surge de processos fragmentados: aprovações via aplicativos de mensagem, compras feitas por um único cartão corporativo compartilhado, reembolsos que chegam semanas depois do gasto. O resultado é um painel financeiro que reflete o passado, não o presente. Mas o uso de cartão virtual corporativo PJ com limites individuais resolve a questão. Cada colaborador opera com o limite correto para sua função e o time financeiro enxerga cada transação no momento em que ela acontece, sem atraso, sem planilhas paralelas. A visibilidade síncrona do painel financeiro também atua diretamente na mitigação de fraudes, tornando anomalias detectáveis antes do fechamento mensal. Responsabilização, Sustentabilidade e Integridade sem atrito operacional A responsabilização (accountability) no contexto de despesas corporativas exige que cada transação tenha uma trilha documental confiável: nota fiscal válida, aprovação registrada e associação clara a um centro de custo e um responsável. Parece simples – e é, quando a infraestrutura é adequada. O problema do modelo clássico de reembolso é a fragilidade documental. Notas fiscais rasuradas, comprovantes de cartão pessoal sem identificação de categoria, aprovações informais que não deixam registro, tudo isso cria buracos na prestação de contas que, em uma auditoria formal, precisarão ser explicados. E explicações sem evidências custam caro: em tempo, em multas e em credibilidade. A integridade fecha esse ciclo: cada gasto precisa estar associado não apenas a uma pessoa, mas a uma política de despesas definida, livre de conflitos de interesse e coerente com os valores declarados pela empresa. Isso inclui regras sobre o que pode ser comprado, em quais categorias e com quais tetos. Quando essas regras existem apenas no papel e não estão parametrizadas nos sistemas financeiros, o controle depende de boa vontade, não de estrutura. Já a sustentabilidade entra na equação quando a empresa consegue enxergar como esses gastos impactam sua saúde financeira no curto, médio e longo prazo; não apenas no fechamento do mês, mas na trajetória do negócio. O calcanhar de Aquiles do compliance: por que o modelo tradicional de reembolso falha em auditorias das Big Four? O processo de reembolso por planilha tem uma grande fragilidade: ele é retroativo. O gasto acontece, o colaborador paga do próprio bolso, a nota fiscal é acumulada, o formulário é preenchido dias depois, o gestor aprova, o financeiro processa. Em cada etapa desse fluxo, há espaço para perda de documentação, divergência de categorias e inserção de dados com imprecisão. Em uma auditoria conduzida por companhias como Deloitte, PwC, EY ou KPMG, esse modelo gera inconsistências graves. Os auditores comparam os lançamentos contábeis com os extratos bancários e, quando os dados não batem ou a documentação está incompleta, o risco fiscal se materializa. Além disso, o uso de contas bancárias pessoais de colaboradores para despesas corporativas é um passivo tributário específico: a Receita Federal pode questionar a natureza dessas movimentações e exigir comprovação de que não se trata de renda adicional não declarada. A conciliação bancária automatizada é a solução direta para esse problema. Em vez de reconciliar dados depois, muitas vezes semanas após o fechamento do período, sistemas integrados permitem que cada transação seja conciliada no momento em que ocorre, eliminando o acúmulo no fechamento mensal e reduzindo o risco de relatórios inconsistentes. Como cartões corporativos individuais por API atuam como ferramentas ativas de governança A diferença entre um cartão corporativo convencional e uma solução gerida por API é a capacidade de parametrização em tempo real. Com o Cartão Corporativo do Stark Bank , o time financeiro não apenas emite cartões individuais, como também pode definir regras de uso para cada usuário ou categoria. Isso significa que é possível criar um cartão destinado exclusivamente a compras de mídia digital, com limite de R$ 50.000 mensais e bloqueio automático para qualquer MCC (Código de Categoria de Comerciante) fora desse escopo. Ou criar um cartão de viagens com teto diário definido, válido apenas durante o período de uma conferência. E essas parametrizações não dependem de aprovações manuais a cada compra, são configuradas uma vez e aplicadas automaticamente. O resultado prático está na tabela abaixo: Diferencial Operacional Sistemas de Reembolso Tradicionais Modelo Stark Bank Rastreabilidade de Gastos Retroativa, via notas acumuladas e planilhas manuais propensas a erros. Síncrona, com dados de transação gerados em tempo real direto no painel do banco. Mitigação de Fraudes Baixa, dependente de auditoria humana amostral pós-despesa. Alta, com regras de gastos pré-aprovadas, bloqueios instantâneos e validação via API. Conciliação Contábil Demorada, com fechamento contábil de até 15 dias após o período. Instantânea, alimentada por webhooks em tempo real integrados ao sistema contábil. Controle por Centro de Custos: organização contábil preventiva Um dos maiores gargalos no fechamento contábil de empresas em crescimento é a categorização retroativa de despesas. Quando os gastos não estão associados a um centro de custos no momento da transação, alguém precisa fazer isso depois e ainda manualmente. Já a segmentação preventiva resolve isso. Ao emitir cartões individuais já vinculados a centros de custo específicos, como Marketing, Recursos Humanos, Operações ou TI, cada gasto é automaticamente categorizado no instante em que ocorre. O orçamento de cada área é consumido em tempo real, e o time financeiro pode identificar desvios antes do fechamento do período, não durante. Para empresas com múltiplas filiais ou unidades de negócio, essa estrutura é ainda mais relevante: ela permite consolidar dados de diferentes operações sem depender de planilhas regionais enviadas por e-mail, reduzindo sensivelmente o tempo gasto na consolidação dos dados fiscais. Integração de despesas corporativas ao sistema de gestão: automação sem atrito contábi l O sistema de gestão empresarial é o núcleo contábil de qualquer empresa de médio e grande porte. O problema é que, no modelo tradicional, os dados de despesas chegam ao ERP com atraso: lançados manualmente, importados de planilhas ou digitados por um analista no fechamento do mês. Já a integração via webhooks muda esse fluxo por completo. A cada transação realizada com o controle de gastos corporativos com cartão , um evento é gerado em tempo real e enviado diretamente ao ERP da empresa. O lançamento acontece automaticamente, com as categorias e centros de custo já definidos. O impacto no processo de fechamento mensal é significativo: o acúmulo de consolidação cai, as divergências entre extrato bancário e sistema contábil desaparecem e a empresa entra no próximo período com os dados já conciliados. Para times financeiros essa mudança representa horas de trabalho recuperadas por ciclo. Impacto da Reforma Tributária: como manter a conformidade fiscal das despesas A Emenda Constitucional 132, promulgada em dezembro de 2023, instituiu a mais ampla reforma tributária do Brasil em décadas. A partir de 2026, o modelo atual de tributação sobre o consumo começa a ser substituído pelo novo Imposto sobre Valor Adicionado (IVA) dual: o Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços (IBS), de competência estadual e municipal, e a Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS), de competência federal. Para a gestão de despesas corporativas, a mudança traz uma exigência prática imediata: rastreabilidade documental de cada transação. A apuração de créditos tributários sob o novo modelo depende da vinculação entre nota fiscal eletrônica, transação bancária e registro contábil. Sem essa trilha completa e auditável, a empresa pode perder o direito a creditamentos que reduzem a carga tributária efetiva. Ou seja, a digitalização de documentos associada a cada transação passa a ser uma exigência legal. Assim, sistemas que capturam a nota fiscal no momento do gasto e a vinculam automaticamente à transação do cartão eliminam o risco de perda de documentação e garantem prontidão para a apuração de créditos sob as novas regras. Como implementar a governança de despesas com a infraestrutura do Stark Bank O Stark Bank é regulado pelo Banco Central do Brasil e é a primeira fintech do país a contar com avaliações das três principais agências globais de rating: S&P (brA-o), Moody’s e Fitch Ratings. Para CFOs que precisam justificar a escolha de um parceiro financeiro perante comitês de auditoria e conselheiros, esses critérios são diferenciais. A infraestrutura do Stark Bank permite implementar governança de despesas de ponta a ponta: emissão de múltiplos cartões corporativos com limites individuais, parametrização de regras por API, segmentação por centro de custos, integração com ERP via webhooks e captura de comprovantes em tempo real. Para scaleups que precisam escalar sem perder o controle e para enterprises que precisam manter o compliance em ambientes de auditoria rigorosa, essa combinação reduz a demanda operacional e garante prontidão para auditorias, sem depender de processos manuais ou planilhas paralelas. Se o seu time financeiro ainda enfrenta esses gargalos na gestão das despesas corporativas, esse é o momento de estruturar uma governança de verdade. Conheça o Stark Bank e descubra como implementar controles de gastos em tempo real na sua empresa. Perguntas frequentes sobre governança corporativa e compliance Qual é o papel da governança corporativa no compliance de despesas PJ? A governança define as regras de autorização de gastos de forma preventiva: quem pode gastar, quanto, em quê e com quais aprovações. O compliance garante que essas transações estejam em conformidade com os órgãos reguladores e com a política interna da empresa. Na prática, governança sem compliance é política sem evidência; compliance sem governança é auditoria sem estrutura de controle. Os dois precisam funcionar juntos. Como os cartões corporativos ajudam na preparação para auditorias das Big Four? O principal argumento em uma auditoria formal é a trilha digital. Cartões corporativos individuais com controles por API geram uma trilha de auditoria completa: data, valor, estabelecimento, categoria, responsável e centro de custo, tudo registrado no momento da transação. Isso elimina as divergências entre os dados bancários e os relatórios contábeis que auditores identificam como risco em modelos de reembolso manual.

title: How to Use AI Assistants to Build a Voice Call Automation | Circle
summary: Learn how to build a voice call automation with Circle Agent Wallet, AI assistants, and USDC to pay for services, place calls, and return proof of execution.
body_text: Agent workflows are easy to execute when they only generate text. They become harder when the agent needs to complete a real task end to end: find a service, pay for it, use it, and return proof of what happened. That is where many developer workflows break. The model may know the next step, but the application still depends on manual setup: creating accounts, adding payment methods, managing API keys, buying credits, checking balances, and stitching together receipts. Circle Agent Wallet helps developers build more autonomous applications by giving agents the ability to pay for services with USDC as a part of their workflow. Instead of relying on a subscription set up ahead of time, the agent can pay for access when it needs it. This unlocks composable workflows where agents can discover, purchase, and consume services on demand Consider a workflow where an AI agent monitors market conditions and needs to notify you immediately when sentiment changes. An email or dashboard notification may be too easy to miss, so the agent decides to place a phone call instead. To complete that task autonomously, it needs to acquire or reuse a phone number, pay for a voice API, initiate the call, and then return the call transcript, recording URL, and payment details. Rather than requiring a preconfigured account with the voice provider, the agent can pay for the service with USDC at the moment it needs it, allowing the entire workflow to execute autonomously from start to finish. Circle Agent Wallet works across AI coding tools and agent runtimes that can run Circle CLI commands or integrate Circle APIs. In this tutorial, we use Codex and Circle Agent Wallet to build that workflow end to end. You will build a workflow that: uses Circle Agent Wallet to pay for the services needed to place a call delivers a short market sentiment update to your phone returns the transcript, recording URL, and spend details for review runs the flow as a thread-bound heartbeat automation in Codex TL;DR setup If you want to try it first and read the breakdown after, start with this prompt in Codex: Use Circle Agent Wallet to set up a recurring voice-call workflow in this Codex thread. Config: - Your email: <EMAIL> - Destination phone: <PHONE_NUMBER> - Schedule: <SCHEDULE> - Auto top-up: 0.65 USDC per run, only if needed - Spending limits: calls up to $0.54 are approved; phone numbers up to $5.00 are approved only during setup; ask before anything higher or different. Goal: Call the destination with a short crypto market sentiment brief, then return transcript, recording URL, call status, and spend details. Setup: 1. Check Circle CLI is installed. 2. Check Circle Agent Wallet auth; if needed, start login and ask me for OTP. 3. List my Base Agent Wallet address. 4. Check Base USDC, service-chain USDC, and Circle Gateway balances. 5. Search for a paid voice-call service that supports my destination number; do not assume Base works for all countries. 6. Reuse an active wallet-owned phone number if available. If none exists, estimate cost and ask before buying. 7. Estimate call cost. 8. Place one short test call only after I confirm. Call style: Short, clear, neutral crypto market sentiment brief. Avoid hype. End cleanly. Max 1 minute. After the first successful call: Create a thread-bound heartbeat automation for the schedule above, continuing this same chat context. On each heartbeat: 1. Re-check auth, wallet address, balances, Gateway balance, caller ID, and call price. 2. Auto top-up only within the configured top-up limit if Gateway is low. 3. Place exactly one scheduled call if all checks pass. 4. Pause and ask if auth expired, terms are required, funds are insufficient, price changed, or phone number purchase/renewal is needed. 5. Return wallet status, services used, paid ledger, caller ID, call ID, status, transcript, recording URL, and total spend. Do not accept terms, buy/renew numbers outside setup, exceed spending limits, or place extra calls without required confirmation. The rest of this guide explains how the setup works and what to expect. Why Circle Agent Wallet is part of this workflow Without a wallet, a workflow like this usually breaks into separate manual steps: sign up for a telephony provider add a payment method buy a phone number provision the service trigger the call track what was spent Circle Agent Wallet changes that by giving the agent a way to hold USDC , apply spending limits, and pay for services in the flow of the task. Because USDC is programmable, the agent can acquire resources and complete work without a human manually provisioning every account or payment step. Prerequisites Before you begin, make sure you have: Access to the Codex app Automations available in Codex Node.js v20.18.2 or later Circle CLI installed A Circle Agent Wallet with up to 6 USDC available on Base or the chain required by the selected service A Circle Gateway balance, or a USDC wallet balance to top up Gateway when needed. Some paid services may use Circle Gateway for payment. Gateway is separate from your wallet balance: your wallet holds USDC onchain, while Gateway can make that USDC available for fast service payments across supported chains. Circle Agent Wallets require human authentication for key actions—including creating a wallet and adding or updating spending policies—to ensure agents operate within user-defined rules and controls. Authentication is email OTP-based, and sessions expire after 28 days, so the initial setup and periodic re-authentication will require your input. Step 1: Set up your Circle Agent Wallet Install Circle CLI: npm install -g @circle-fin/cli Authenticate your wallet: circle wallet login [email protected] Get your wallet address on Base: circle wallet list --type agent --chain BASE Fund the wallet with USDC: circle wallet fund --address 0xYourWalletAddress --chain BASE --amount 10 --method crypto Check the balance: circle wallet balance --address 0xYourWalletAddress --chain BASE Step 2: Understand how the payment step works Circle CLI supports x402 -compatible paid requests with: circle services pay <url> --address 0xYourWalletAddress --chain <SERVICE_CHAIN> The service chain depends on the provider. For example, A voice-call service may accept payments on Polygon even if your Agent Wallet is funded on Base. Circle Gateway’s unified balance handles the crosschain transfer automatically. For this voice workflow, those paid steps may include: checking or reusing a wallet-owned phone number buying a phone number if no active one exists topping up Circle Gateway for nanopayments placing the outbound call Step 3: Run the prompt in Codex Now ask Codex to set up the workflow. The prompt should tell Codex to: check that Circle CLI and Circle Agent Wallet are ready find a voice-call service that can call your phone number reuse an existing wallet-owned caller ID, or ask before buying one estimate costs before paying place one short test call only after you confirm return the call transcript, recording URL, status, and spend details create a thread-bound heartbeat automation after the first successful call A simplified starter prompt looks like this: Use Circle Agent Wallet to set up a recurring voice-call workflow in this Codex thread. Call <PHONE_NUMBER> with a short crypto market sentiment brief. First check that Circle CLI, wallet auth, wallet balances, and Circle Gateway are ready. Find a paid voice-call service that supports the destination number. Reuse an active wallet-owned caller ID if available, or ask before buying one. Before placing the first call, estimate the phone-number and call costs, then ask me to confirm. After a successful test call, create a thread-bound heartbeat automation for <SCHEDULE> so future runs continue from this same chat context. Each run should return wallet status, services used, paid-call ledger, caller ID, call ID, call status, transcript, recording URL, and total spend. Keep the call short, neutral, and hype-free. Do not accept terms, buy or renew numbers, fund the wallet, exceed expected costs, or place calls unless confirmation is required and given. Step 4: Turn the task into a thread-bound heartbeat After the first successful call, create a thread-bound heartbeat automation, not a separate cron automation. This keeps future runs in the same Codex chat context, so the workflow can reuse discovered states like the wallet address, caller ID, provider endpoint, payment chain, and spending policy. Step 5: Review the call outputs A strong run should return: wallet status services used paid-call ledger purchased phone number call ID transcript recording URL total spend What success looks like A good run should feel simple from your side: Codex checks whether the wallet is ready Codex finds and pays for the required services Codex places the call you receive the update Codex returns the transcript, recording URL, and spend summary Alternative patterns For recurring market briefings, you can run the workflow every morning or every week with different prompts. For escalation workflows, you can trigger the call only when something important happens. Wrapping up In this tutorial, you used an AI development tool and Circle Agent Wallet to build a recurring voice call automation that can pay for the resources it needs, place a call, and return the resulting artifacts for review. This is the larger shift behind agent commerce: agents are moving from planning work to completing work. Programmable USDC gives agents a way to acquire services, operate within user-defined spending limits, and return payment records as part of the task. title: Superblock Work Hubs for Jakarta Teams
summary: Jakarta’s workday is being redesigned around mixed-use districts Anyone who has crossed Jakarta between meetings knows the real cost of “just one more trip.” A short calendar gap can disappear into traffic, parking queues, lobby check-ins, and the mental reset needed before the next call. For professionals, founders, sales teams, and regional business travelers in […] The post Superblock Work Hubs for Jakarta Teams appeared first on Deskimo .
body_text: Jakarta’s workday is being redesigned around mixed-use districts Anyone who has crossed Jakarta between meetings knows the real cost of “just one more trip.” A short calendar gap can disappear into traffic, parking queues, lobby check-ins, and the mental reset needed before the next call. For professionals, founders, sales teams, and regional business travelers in Indonesia, the smarter question is no longer “Where is the office?” but “Where should work happen today?” That is where superblock hubs are becoming a practical workplace trend. Jakarta’s integrated districts combine offices, malls, apartments, hotels, transit access, gyms, clinics, and dining in one compact environment. Used well, these hubs can reduce wasted travel time, support hybrid teams, and give employees better places to focus between client visits, internal meetings, and deep work sessions. Why superblock hubs fit Jakarta’s workplace reality Jakarta has always been a city of movement, but not all movement creates business value. Teams often travel from home to headquarters, then to a client site, then back across town for an internal meeting. Each transfer adds friction, especially during peak commuting windows or rainy-season congestion. Superblock hubs help teams rethink the workday around proximity. Instead of treating the central office as the default destination, companies can create a network of approved work locations inside mixed-use districts close to employees, clients, and transit corridors. Jakarta’s commute challenge is a productivity issue Traffic is not just an urban inconvenience; it affects how many meetings can be held, how much focused work gets done, and how employees feel at the end of the day. The TomTom Traffic Index for Jakarta regularly places the city among the more congested major urban areas, making travel planning a real operational concern for businesses. For HR leaders and department heads, this turns location strategy into a performance lever. If a team can replace a 90-minute cross-city commute with a 15-minute walk from a client meeting to a workspace inside the same district, the gain is immediate. The same principle applies to business travelers arriving from Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Tokyo, or Bali. A visitor with meetings in Sudirman, Kuningan, or Senayan may not need a full-day office. They need a reliable desk, meeting room, call booth, and stable connectivity within reach of their schedule. Mixed-use districts match how modern teams actually work Jakarta’s business activity is increasingly clustered around integrated districts such as Sudirman Central Business District, Kuningan, Thamrin, Senayan, Kelapa Gading, Puri, and areas connected to MRT or LRT routes. These locations already support the daily routines of professionals who combine meetings, meals, errands, and focused work. Strong superblock hubs typically offer: Office towers, coworking spaces, and serviced workspaces within walking distance Food and beverage options suitable for informal meetings or quick team lunches Retail, banking, clinics, fitness centers, and daily services that reduce side trips Hotels or serviced residences for visiting executives and regional teams Better access to ride-hailing pick-up points, MRT stations, TransJakarta corridors, or parking facilities When a district supports both work and life needs, employees spend less time coordinating logistics and more time doing the work they were hired to do. How superblock hubs improve hybrid team performance Hybrid work in Indonesia is no longer only about working from home. For many teams, the more useful model is distributed access: employees choose the most suitable professional workspace based on their tasks, meetings, and location for the day. Superblock hubs make this model easier to manage because they provide a familiar, repeatable structure. A sales team can meet prospects near the client’s office, a product team can gather for a sprint review near a transit-connected mall, and a manager can book a quiet room for performance conversations without asking employees to travel to headquarters. Use hubs to cut dead time between meetings One of the biggest workplace inefficiencies in Jakarta is the “in-between” hour. It is too short to return to the office, too long to waste in a café, and often too noisy for serious work. Superblock hubs solve this by giving professionals a predictable place to reset. For example, a B2B account manager may start the morning with a client in Mega Kuningan, take a video call from a nearby workspace, meet a prospect over lunch, and finish proposals before heading home. The day stays productive because the work environment follows the route. This approach is closely related to the idea of placing workspaces near clients rather than forcing everyone back to a single hub. For more on this operational shift, see how near-client workspaces cut dead time . Create a better employee experience without overbuilding offices Employees value flexibility, but they also need professional settings. Working from home may be effective for individual tasks, yet it can be difficult for confidential calls, stable video meetings, mentoring sessions, or team collaboration. Cafés are convenient but inconsistent. Superblock hubs offer a middle path. Employees get access to work-ready spaces in locations they already use, while employers avoid the cost and rigidity of leasing large offices in every district. For Indonesia-based teams, this can be especially useful when employees live across Greater Jakarta, including South Tangerang, Bekasi, Depok, and West Jakarta. A distributed workspace plan can reduce unnecessary travel while still giving everyone access to professional infrastructure. Where Jakarta teams can use superblock hubs most effectively Not every workday needs the same type of workspace. The value of superblock hubs comes from matching the location and format to the business need. This helps companies avoid both extremes: forcing all work into one headquarters or allowing unmanaged workspace spending across random venues. For best results, teams should map the most common movement patterns in their organization. Look at where employees live, where clients are concentrated, where leadership meetings happen, and which districts are already part of the team’s weekly routine. Best use cases by team type Different teams benefit from hub-based work in different ways: Sales and account teams: Use work hubs near client clusters to prepare, debrief, and update CRM notes immediately after meetings. HR and people teams: Host interviews, onboarding sessions, and confidential conversations in neutral, accessible locations. Finance and legal teams: Book secure meeting rooms for document-heavy work when privacy matters more than a casual setting. Founders and entrepreneurs: Combine investor meetings, vendor calls, and focused execution days without committing to a permanent office. Regional business travelers: Work productively between hotel check-out, airport transfers, and meetings in different business districts. Freelancers and consultants: Upgrade from cafés to professional spaces when meeting clients or handling intensive project work. For companies with hybrid teams, the most successful patterns often start with one or two use cases. For example, a company may first approve hubs for client-facing teams, then expand access to project teams that need occasional collaboration space. District selection matters more than office size A common mistake is judging workspace strategy by square meters alone. In Jakarta, accessibility can be more important than size. A smaller workspace in the right superblock may outperform a larger office that requires long travel from clients or employees. When evaluating locations, consider: Distance to major clients, partners, and government offices Proximity to MRT Jakarta, TransJakarta, commuter rail, or reliable ride-hailing access Availability of quiet call areas and meeting rooms, not just open desks Food, prayer room, parking, and daily convenience facilities Safety, building quality, and ease of navigation for visitors Whether the district remains usable during peak hours and bad weather Jakarta’s transport development continues to influence where work happens. Companies can monitor official updates from the Jakarta Provincial Government and transport-related agencies to understand how infrastructure improvements may change commuting and workspace demand over time. Building a cost-smart strategy around superblock hubs Workspace flexibility becomes much more powerful when it is managed deliberately. Without a plan, employees may expense cafés, hotel lounges, day passes, and ad hoc meeting rooms in ways that are difficult to track. This creates hidden costs and inconsistent employee experiences. A good hub strategy gives teams freedom within clear boundaries. Employees know where they can work, managers know how budgets are used, and finance teams can see whether flexible workspace spending is replacing or simply adding to existing office costs. Turn scattered spending into visible workplace data Many companies underestimate how much they already spend on informal work locations. Small reimbursements may look harmless individually, but they add up across teams and months. They can also hide risk if employees handle confidential work in unsecured public settings. Common sources of hidden workplace spend include: Café bills used as unofficial workspace expenses Hotel lobby meetings for visiting teams One-off coworking day passes booked without approval Meeting rooms paid by individual departments Extra transport costs caused by unnecessary office returns If this sounds familiar, it may be worth reviewing how shadow workspace spend appears in hybrid teams . The goal is not to reduce flexibility, but to make it accountable. In a market like Jakarta, visible usage data can reveal which districts truly support productivity. If employees consistently book spaces in Kuningan, Sudirman, or Puri because those areas align with client visits, the company can adjust policy based on real behavior rather than assumptions. Compare hub access with traditional office expansion Leasing a full office can still make sense for headquarters functions, culture-building, and teams that need daily co-location. But for companies expanding across Jakarta or Indonesia, permanent leases in every strategic district may be inefficient. Superblock hubs work well when demand is real but variable. For example, a team may need eight desks in South Jakarta on Tuesdays, a meeting room in Central Jakarta twice a month, and occasional quiet space near the airport or a hotel district for visiting leaders. A flexible model handles these patterns without locking the company into unused capacity. This is similar to the financial logic behind fractional offices. While the market context differs, the cost-control principle is useful for Indonesian decision-makers too. Read how fractional offices support cost control to see how flexible access can complement permanent office commitments. Companies can also benchmark workplace decisions against broader economic indicators. The Statistics Indonesia site provides data that can help leaders understand employment, urbanization, and economic trends shaping workforce planning. How to implement a hub-based workplace policy Moving to a hub-based model does not require a dramatic office transformation. The best implementation usually starts with a focused pilot, clear rules, and regular review. This lets companies learn from actual usage before scaling across departments. The policy should be simple enough for employees to use and structured enough for managers to govern. If the process is too complicated, teams will return to informal habits. If it is too loose, the company loses visibility. Start with a 60-day pilot A practical pilot helps organizations validate demand before making larger decisions. Choose a few teams that travel frequently or struggle with long commutes. Sales, customer success, recruitment, and project teams are often good candidates. A 60-day pilot can include: Two to four approved districts based on client proximity and employee commute patterns Clear booking rules for desks, meeting rooms, and private call spaces Monthly budget limits by team or role Guidelines for confidential calls and document handling Feedback surveys on productivity, commute time, and workspace quality Usage reporting to compare actual demand with expectations At the end of the pilot, review both quantitative and qualitative signals. Look at booking frequency, popular locations, average session length, employee satisfaction, and whether transport claims changed. A successful pilot should show either time savings, better meeting outcomes, improved employee experience, or clearer cost visibility. Design rules that support trust and accountability Employees are more likely to use flexible workspace responsibly when expectations are clear. Avoid vague instructions such as “use when needed.” Instead, define the situations where hub access is encouraged. For example, companies may approve superblock hubs when employees: Have two or more client meetings in the same district Need a quiet place for video calls between external appointments Are attending a team workshop or offsite collaboration session Need a professional setting for interviews or performance conversations Are traveling from another Indonesian city and need a temporary work base It also helps to clarify when employees should not use paid workspace, such as for short personal errands, purely social meetings, or work that can be done effectively from home without disruption. Clear policy does not reduce autonomy. It protects it by making the model sustainable. What Jakarta can learn from regional workspace trends Jakarta is not alone in rethinking where professional work happens. Across Asia, dense cities are using malls, mixed-use developments, and transit-linked districts as flexible work nodes. The details vary by market, but the direction is clear: work is moving closer to daily life. This shift matters for Indonesia because Jakarta teams often balance global expectations with local realities. They need responsive workplace models that support international clients, regional travel, and domestic growth while recognizing congestion, neighborhood diversity, and employee wellbeing. Retail-integrated work is becoming a serious business tool Malls and mixed-use complexes are no longer just shopping destinations. In many Asian cities, they are becoming practical work environments because they offer safety, accessibility, food, parking, and extended operating hours. For employees, this reduces the friction of planning a full workday around multiple needs. The trend is especially visible in places where space is expensive and commuting is time-consuming. Hong Kong offers a useful comparison, where mall-connected work hubs help teams stay productive in dense urban districts. See how mall work hubs support Hong Kong teams for a regional perspective that Jakarta companies can adapt. For Jakarta, the opportunity is to use superblock hubs as part of a wider workplace ecosystem. Headquarters can remain important for culture and leadership, while flexible hubs handle distributed execution, client proximity, and intermittent collaboration. The future is not office versus remote; it is location intelligence The most effective workplace strategies will not simply ask employees to return to the office or stay home. They will use location intelligence to decide where different types of work happen best. That may mean: Deep work from home or a quiet nearby hub Client preparation from a workspace close to the meeting location Team rituals at headquarters on fixed days Leadership reviews in private rooms near central transit Regional visitor support through on-demand workspace access This model is especially relevant in Indonesia, where teams may be spread across Greater Jakarta and increasingly connected to clients across Southeast Asia. Superblock hubs give companies a practical way to support that complexity without overcommitting to fixed real estate. Make each workday easier to plan, easier to manage, and easier to justify For Jakarta teams, the best workplace strategy is not necessarily the biggest office or the most flexible policy. It is the one that reduces friction while keeping people productive, connected, and accountable. Superblock hubs offer a strong fit because they align with how the city already functions: business districts, malls, residences, hotels, and transport links working together in compact urban ecosystems. For employees, this means fewer wasted hours and more professional places to focus. For managers, it means better support for hybrid work without losing visibility. For finance and operations teams, it creates a clearer alternative to unmanaged workspace spend and underused office space. Start small, choose the right districts, measure real usage, and build a policy that reflects the way your people actually move through Jakarta. Done well, superblock hubs can turn the city’s complexity into a workplace advantage for teams across Indonesia. To book a workspace or download the free Deskimo app . title: Founder-Led Marketing: How B2B Startups Turn Founder Expertise Into Pipeline
summary: Founder-led marketing works when founder expertise becomes a repeatable content and distribution system, not random posts or delegated AI slop.
body_text: Founder-Led Marketing: How B2B Startups Turn Founder Expertise Into Pipeline Founder-led marketing is not a founder posting whenever they have a launch, a thought, or a spare 20 minutes. It is a system for turning the founder's expertise, customer insight, category point of view, and hard-won lessons into distribution that builds trust before the first sales call. That distinction matters. Most B2B startups do founder-led marketing badly because they treat it like a content task. Write a post. Approve a caption. Share a funding announcement. Move on. The founders who make it work treat it like a growth channel. They capture the thinking that already happens inside the business, turn it into sharp content, distribute it through the founder profile, and connect it back to pipeline. That is the difference between sounding visible and becoming trusted. ‍ What Founder-Led Marketing Actually Means Founder-led marketing is the practice of using the founder's expertise and public point of view to create demand, build trust, and move buyers closer to action. It is not the same thing as personal branding. Personal branding is often about recognition. Founder-led marketing is about commercial trust. The founder is not posting to become internet famous. The founder is posting because buyers, investors, partners, and future hires want to understand how the company thinks before they commit attention, budget, or reputation. In a B2B market where every company can publish generic content, the founder's lived experience is the part competitors cannot clone. The sales calls. The product tradeoffs. The customer objections. The market lessons. The unpopular beliefs. The moments where the company chose one path and rejected another. That is the raw material. A strong founder-led marketing system turns that raw material into: LinkedIn posts that build trust with the right buyers Long-form articles that rank, educate, and convert Comments and conversations that put the founder inside the right networks Sales enablement assets that answer objections before a call Investor and recruiting visibility that compounds over time If you already have a founder content strategy , founder-led marketing is the go-to-market layer around it. It connects the content system to distribution, trust, and pipeline. ‍ Why B2B Startups Need the Founder in the Market Early and growth-stage B2B companies do not win because the market fully understands them. They win because a small group of high-intent people starts to trust their judgment before everyone else catches up. That trust rarely starts with a company page. It starts with a person. Buyers want to know what the founder sees that others miss. Investors want to know whether the founder has a sharp read on the category. Future employees want to know whether the company has conviction or just a roadmap. Partners want to know whether the team is credible enough to bet on. Founder-led marketing gives all of those audiences a clearer signal. It also solves a practical distribution problem. Company content often feels sanitized. Founder content can be specific, opinionated, and context-rich. That does not mean reckless. It means the content carries a real point of view instead of sounding like it was approved by five departments. For Series A and later B2B startups, this becomes especially important. Paid ads get more expensive. Cold outbound gets noisier. PR is sporadic. The founder's LinkedIn presence becomes one of the few channels where credibility and distribution can compound together. That is why the question is not whether the founder should be visible. The question is how to make that visibility operational without turning the founder into a full-time creator. ‍ The Mistake: Delegating the Voice Before Capturing the Thinking The fastest way to ruin founder-led marketing is to outsource the voice before anyone has captured the thinking. This is where generic AI slop and cheap ghostwriting usually fail. A writer cannot invent a founder's judgment. A tool cannot guess the nuance behind a product decision. A content calendar cannot create conviction where the input is a vague topic like "share thoughts on the market." The founder does not need to write every word. But the founder does need to supply the substance. That substance usually already exists. It is hiding in places like: Customer calls where the founder explains the problem better than the website does Sales objections that reveal what the market misunderstands Investor updates with sharp category observations Internal Slack messages where strategy is explained clearly Product debates that expose the company's actual beliefs Recruiting conversations where the founder tells the real story The system should capture those moments, not ask the founder to stare at a blank page every week. This is why the best founder-led marketing process starts with extraction. Voice memos. Interview calls. Meeting notes. Draft approvals. Short comments from the founder that sharpen the argument. Once the thinking is captured, a strong content team can turn it into publishable work. Without that capture layer, the output may be polished, but it will not sound earned. ‍ A Practical Founder-Led Marketing System A founder-led marketing system needs four parts: capture, shape, distribute, and convert. Miss one, and the channel becomes inconsistent. Hit all four, and the founder's expertise starts working even when the founder is not actively posting. ‍ 1. Capture the Founder's Raw Expertise The capture layer is where ideas enter the system. Do not start with a list of post topics. Start with the places where the founder is already useful. Sales calls, customer interviews, investor conversations, product reviews, board prep, and internal debates are all better inputs than trend lists. A simple weekly capture process is enough for most founders: One 30-minute interview with the founder Three to five voice notes after meaningful calls A shared note for strong opinions, objections, and examples A quick review of sales and customer questions The goal is not to create more work. The goal is to stop letting valuable thinking disappear. ‍ 2. Shape the Ideas Into Repeatable Content Formats Raw expertise needs structure before it becomes useful content. For founder-led marketing, the strongest formats usually include: Belief posts: what the founder thinks the market gets wrong Lesson posts: what the founder learned from a real decision Objection posts: how to reframe a common buyer concern Framework posts: how the founder thinks through a problem Proof posts: what changed for a customer, team, or product Comparison posts: why one channel, category, or strategy works differently than another These formats prevent the founder from sounding random. They also make approval easier because everyone knows what kind of argument the piece is trying to make. If the content is mostly for LinkedIn, pair these formats with a clear LinkedIn content strategy for founders . The point is not just to post more. The point is to build repeated market memory around a few ideas the founder wants to own. ‍ 3. Distribute Through the Founder Profile Distribution is where most B2B teams underuse the founder. They publish a company blog post, share it once from the company page, and wonder why nothing happens. The founder profile should be the first distribution layer because people follow people before they follow companies. A single founder post can create conversation, reach second-degree networks, and surface the company's point of view in a way a brand post usually cannot. But distribution is not only posting. It also includes strategic commenting, replying to thoughtful comments, sending useful follow-ups, and turning strong posts into longer assets. A practical weekly rhythm looks like this: Two to three founder LinkedIn posts tied to core business themes One long-form article or SEO asset per week or every other week Daily comment blocks on ICP-relevant posts Repurposing the best-performing post into newsletter, blog, or sales copy Tagging content by theme so the team can reuse it later This is where a platform and workflow matter. Without calendars, approvals, reminders, scheduling, and analytics, founder-led marketing becomes a recurring fire drill. ‍ 4. Convert Attention Into Pipeline Founder-led marketing should create trust, but trust still needs a path. Every content system needs conversion points. Not aggressive pitches in every post. Clear next steps for readers who are already leaning in. Those next steps can include: A relevant internal link to a deeper guide A soft CTA to book a conversation A newsletter or content audit offer A useful resource for the buyer's current problem A sales follow-up triggered by a qualified comment or profile view The best conversion path depends on the reader's stage. Someone reading a broad founder-led marketing guide may need education. Someone reading a LinkedIn ROI breakdown may be closer to evaluating whether the channel is worth operationalizing. The job of the system is to meet both without forcing every reader into the same CTA. ‍ Founder-Led Marketing vs. Hiring a Content Marketer At some point, the founder asks a reasonable question: should we just hire someone in-house? Sometimes, yes. But hiring a content marketer does not automatically solve founder-led marketing. A marketer can manage calendars, briefs, analytics, publishing, and repurposing. Those are important. But the hard part is still extracting the founder's specific judgment and translating it into content that buyers trust. If the founder is unavailable, the marketer becomes a guesser. If the marketer is too junior, the content becomes generic. If the process lacks approvals, the founder becomes a bottleneck. If the company hires before the strategy is clear, the new hire inherits chaos. For many Series A+ founders, the better move is to build the system first: Clear positioning Repeatable idea capture Founder voice guidelines Content pillars tied to pipeline Approval workflows that fit the founder's schedule Distribution and engagement rhythms Then decide whether to run it with an in-house hire, an agency partner, or a hybrid model. This is the gap a ghostwriting system for founders can close when it is done correctly. The point is not to fake the founder's voice. The point is to make the founder's thinking easier to ship. ‍ Where LinkedIn Fits in Founder-Led Marketing LinkedIn is usually the best starting point because the audience is already professional, searchable, and commercially relevant. For B2B founders, LinkedIn does three jobs at once. First, it builds familiarity with buyers before they enter an active evaluation. Second, it gives investors and partners a public record of how the founder thinks. Third, it creates a distribution surface for blog posts, product narratives, hiring stories, and category opinions. But LinkedIn should not be isolated from the rest of the content engine. The best founder-led marketing systems connect LinkedIn to SEO, sales, and employee distribution. A founder post can become a blog section. A blog post can become five LinkedIn posts. A strong comment thread can become a sales objection asset. A company-wide amplification system can turn one founder point of view into broader market reach. That is why LinkedIn employee advocacy works best when it starts with a founder-led point of view. The team should not be forced to amplify generic company updates. They should be given sharp ideas worth sharing. ‍ What to Measure Founder-led marketing is easy to undervalue if you only measure the final click. The channel often creates demand before the buyer is ready to be tracked. Someone sees the founder's post, recognizes the name later, reads a blog post, asks a peer about the company, and eventually comes inbound through search or direct traffic. That does not mean measurement is impossible. It means the scoreboard needs to match the channel. Track these signals: ICP profile views: are the right buyers looking at the founder? Qualified inbound conversations: are relevant people starting DMs or replying to posts? Sales-call mentions: are prospects referencing founder content before or during calls? Branded search lift: are more people searching the founder or company by name? Content-assisted pipeline: are deals influenced by content even when attribution credits another channel? Approval speed: can the team ship without chasing the founder every day? The last metric matters more than most teams think. A founder-led content engine that cannot get approvals will not compound. The operational layer is part of the strategy. ‍ The 90-Day Founder-Led Marketing Plan You do not need a huge campaign to start. You need a repeatable operating rhythm. ‍ Days 1-30: Positioning and Capture Define the three to five ideas the founder wants to own. Audit the founder's LinkedIn profile, existing content, sales calls, and strongest customer proof. Set up a weekly interview or voice-note workflow. Decide which content requires founder review and which content can be approved by the team. By the end of the first month, the team should have a backlog of founder-sourced ideas and a clear point of view. ‍ Days 31-60: Publishing and Distribution Start publishing consistently. For most founders, that means two to three LinkedIn posts per week, one longer asset every one to two weeks, and a daily comment habit focused on buyers, investors, partners, or category peers. Use a content calendar, not a spreadsheet graveyard. Every piece should have a theme, owner, status, approval step, and scheduled date. ‍ Days 61-90: Feedback and Pipeline Integration Review what is creating the right conversations. Look at comments, DMs, profile views, sales-call mentions, and traffic to linked assets. Turn strong posts into longer articles. Turn common objections into new content. Add internal links between related pieces so the content library starts to compound. This is where founder-led marketing becomes more than posting. It becomes a learning loop between the market and the company. ‍ The Bottom Line Founder-led marketing works because the founder is often the clearest signal a B2B startup has. Not the logo. Not the tagline. Not the company page. The founder's judgment. The mistake is assuming that judgment has to be manually written from scratch every week. It does not. It needs to be captured, shaped, distributed, approved, and measured through a system that respects the founder's time. That is what Rethoric is built for: founder-led LinkedIn content with the strategy, workflows, approvals, scheduling, engagement, and analytics needed to keep the engine running without turning the founder into the content team. If you want your expertise to become a growth channel instead of another unfinished task, book an intro call with Rethoric . We will map the first 90 days of your founder-led marketing system and show where LinkedIn can start creating pipeline.

body_text: CARMEL, Ind. (July 20, 2026) — Merchants Capital today announced the closing of Merchants Capital Tax Credit Equity Fund 31, a $160 million multi-investor fund with 10 institutional investors. Merchants Fund 31 will infuse equity into nine affordable housing properties that will create or preserve more than 1,400 affordable homes in Rhode Island, Ohio, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, Utah and Michigan. The investors included both bank and economic investors and included seven repeat and three new investors to the Merchants Capital tax credit platform. “The successful closing of Fund 31 reflects the strength of the relationships we have built with our investor partners and their continued confidence in both our firm and the mission of affordable housing,” said Ryan Thompson, Senior Vice President of Syndications and Investor Relations at Merchants Capital. “We are deeply grateful for the trust they place in our team. Together with our development partners, we are investing in communities, expanding housing opportunities and creating lasting impact for families and residents across the country.” “The successful closing of Fund 31 reflects the strength of the relationships we have built with our investor partners and their continued confidence in both our firm and the mission of affordable housing. We are deeply grateful for the trust they place in our team. Together with our development partners, we are investing in communities, expanding housing opportunities and creating lasting impact for families and residents across the country.” Ryan Thompson SVP, Syndications and Investor Relations, Equity The firm’s capital raise, which has now surpassed $3 billion since the platform launched five years ago, comprises approximately $1.3 billion in multi-investor offerings, $1.6 billion in proprietary fund investments and $91 million in state credit syndications. “Together with our partners, our investments have supported construction and preservation of more than 24,600 units of affordable housing in 31 states across more than 200 properties,” said Julie Sharp, President of Equity Investments at Merchants Capital. “It is incredibly rewarding to work alongside such a dedicated team and platform of investors and developers who share our vision of delivering high-quality, stable, safe and affordable housing for all.” “Together with our partners, our investments have supported construction and preservation of more than 24,600 units of affordable housing in 31 states across more than 200 properties. It is incredibly rewarding to work alongside such a dedicated team and platform of investors and developers who share our vision of delivering high-quality, stable, safe and affordable housing for all.” Julie Sharp President, Equity Investments To learn more about Merchants Capital and its services, visit www.MerchantsCapital.com or find Merchants Capital on Facebook , X , LinkedIn and Instagram .
